import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np

# a)
# ii)

data_path="heart_disease.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(data_path)

# drop missing values
df_subset = df.dropna()

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=df_subset, 
    x='thalach', 
    y='oldpeak', 
    hue='target', 
    palette=['#3498db', '#e74c3c'], # Blue for 0, Red for 1
    alpha=0.7,
    edgecolor='k'
)

plt.title('Heart Disease Presence: thalach vs. oldpeak')
plt.xlabel('Maximum Heart Rate Achieved (thalach) [bpm]')
plt.ylabel('ST Depression Induced by Exercise (oldpeak) [mm]')

# Update legend for clarity
handles, labels  =  plt.gca().get_legend_handles_labels()
plt.legend(handles, ['0 (No Disease)', '1 (Disease)'], title='Target')

plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
plt.show()

The data looks somewhat separable by eye. However, there regions of overlap, especially in the lower right corner of the plot.

# ii)
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = df_subset[['thalach', 'oldpeak']].values
y = df_subset['target'].values

np.random.seed(42)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42
)

mu = np.mean(X_train, axis=0)
sigma = np.std(X_train, axis=0)
X_train_scaled = (X_train - mu) / sigma
X_test_scaled = (X_test - mu) / sigma

print(f"Training set mean (before scaling): {mu}")
print(f"Training set std (before scaling): {sigma}")
print(f"Scaled Train mean: {np.mean(X_train_scaled, axis=0)}") # Should be [0, 0]
print(f"Scaled Train std: {np.std(X_train_scaled, axis=0)}")   # Should be [1, 1]

Training set mean (before scaling): [150.09917355   1.03553719]
Training set std (before scaling): [22.42449405  1.18540431]
Scaled Train mean: [ 4.45236134e-16 -2.62875121e-16]
Scaled Train std: [1. 1.]

from sklearn.svm import SVC

svc = SVC(kernel='linear', C=1.0)
svc.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

sns.scatterplot(
    x=X_train_scaled[:, 0], 
    y=X_train_scaled[:, 1], 
    hue=y_train, 
    palette=['#3498db', '#e74c3c'], 
    alpha=0.7, 
    edgecolor='k',
    legend=False
)

plt.scatter(
    svc.support_vectors_[:, 0], 
    svc.support_vectors_[:, 1], 
    s=150, 
    facecolors='none', 
    edgecolors='k', 
    linewidths=1.5,
    label='Support Vectors'
)

ax = plt.gca()
xlim = ax.get_xlim()
ylim = ax.get_ylim()

xx = np.linspace(xlim[0], xlim[1], 50)
yy = np.linspace(ylim[0], ylim[1], 50)
XX, YY = np.meshgrid(xx, yy)
xy = np.vstack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()]).T
Z = svc.decision_function(xy).reshape(XX.shape)

ax.contour(
    XX, YY, Z, 
    colors='k', 
    levels=[-1, 0, 1], 
    alpha=0.8, 
    linestyles=['--', '-', '--']
)

plt.title('Linear SVM: Decision Boundary and Margins')
plt.xlabel('Standardized thalach')
plt.ylabel('Standardized oldpeak')

handles = [
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor='#3498db', markersize=10, label='0 (No Disease)'),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor='#e74c3c', markersize=10, label='1 (Disease)'),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markeredgecolor='k', markerfacecolor='none', markersize=12, markeredgewidth=1.5, label='Support Vectors'),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='k', linestyle='-', label='Decision Boundary'),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='k', linestyle='--', label='Margins')
]
plt.legend(handles=handles, loc='best')

plt.show()

In [23]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(25, 5))
degrees = [2, 3, 5, 7, 9]

#compute min and max for each axis
x_min, x_max = X_train_scaled[:, 0].min() - 1, X_train_scaled[:, 0].max() + 1
y_min, y_max = X_train_scaled[:, 1].min() - 1, X_train_scaled[:, 1].max() + 1
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 200), np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 200))
xy = np.vstack([xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).T

for ax, d in zip(axes, degrees):
    poly_svc = SVC(kernel='poly', degree=d, C=1.0)
    poly_svc.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

    train_acc = poly_svc.score(X_train_scaled, y_train)
    test_acc = poly_svc.score(X_test_scaled, y_test)
    
    print(f"Degree {d} | Train Acc: {train_acc:.4f} | Test Acc: {test_acc:.4f}")
    
    Z = poly_svc.decision_function(xy).reshape(xx.shape)
    
    sns.scatterplot(
        x=X_train_scaled[:, 0], 
        y=X_train_scaled[:, 1], 
        hue=y_train, 
        palette=['#3498db', '#e74c3c'], 
        alpha=0.6,
        edgecolor='k',
        legend=False,
        ax=ax
    )
    
    ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, colors='k', levels=[0], linestyles=['-'])
    ax.set_title(f'Polynomial Degree {d}')
    ax.set_xlabel('Standardized thalach')
    #Only have y-label once
    if d == 2:
        ax.set_ylabel('Standardized oldpeak')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Degree 2 | Train Acc: 0.6364 | Test Acc: 0.5738
Degree 3 | Train Acc: 0.6901 | Test Acc: 0.7049
Degree 5 | Train Acc: 0.6777 | Test Acc: 0.6230
Degree 7 | Train Acc: 0.6818 | Test Acc: 0.6393
Degree 9 | Train Acc: 0.6942 | Test Acc: 0.6393

Higher degree polynomials perform significantly worse in comparison to the linear model. The boundaries start forming unecessary circles and curves to include or exclude individual points. While degrees 2, 3, and 5 could still be relatively acceptable, degrees 7, 9 draw completely unrealistic boundaries that show obvious overfitting.

# d)
gammas = [0.1, 1, 10, 100]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 6))

x_min, x_max = X_train_scaled[:, 0].min() - 1, X_train_scaled[:, 0].max() + 1
y_min, y_max = X_train_scaled[:, 1].min() - 1, X_train_scaled[:, 1].max() + 1
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 200), np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 200))
xy = np.vstack([xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).T

for ax, g in zip(axes.ravel(), gammas):
    rbf_svc = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=g, C=1.0)
    rbf_svc.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
    
    train_acc = rbf_svc.score(X_train_scaled, y_train)
    test_acc = rbf_svc.score(X_test_scaled, y_test)
    
    print(f"Gamma {g:3} | Train Acc: {train_acc:.4f} | Test Acc: {test_acc:.4f}")
    
    Z = rbf_svc.decision_function(xy).reshape(xx.shape)
    
    sns.scatterplot(
        x=X_train_scaled[:, 0], 
        y=X_train_scaled[:, 1], 
        hue=y_train, 
        palette=['#3498db', '#e74c3c'], 
        alpha=0.6,
        edgecolor='k',
        legend=False,
        ax=ax
    )
    
    ax.contour(xx, yy, Z, colors='k', levels=[0], linestyles=['-'])
    ax.set_title(f'RBF Gamma = {g}')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Gamma 0.1 | Train Acc: 0.7397 | Test Acc: 0.7541
Gamma   1 | Train Acc: 0.7355 | Test Acc: 0.8197
Gamma  10 | Train Acc: 0.8017 | Test Acc: 0.6885
Gamma 100 | Train Acc: 0.9215 | Test Acc: 0.7213

The best accuracy is for gamma=10, but it already shows signs of overfitting. Gamma=100 creates ultra specific boundaries, some of which include only one point and cleary overfit our data.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

lr = LogisticRegression()
lr.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.scatterplot(
    x=X_train_scaled[:, 0], 
    y=X_train_scaled[:, 1], 
    hue=y_train, 
    palette=['#3498db', '#e74c3c'], 
    alpha=0.6, 
    edgecolor='k', 
    legend=False
)

ax = plt.gca()
xlim = ax.get_xlim()
ylim = ax.get_ylim()
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(xlim[0], xlim[1], 100), np.linspace(ylim[0], ylim[1], 100))
xy = np.vstack([xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]).T

#get svc from part b i)
Z_svm = svc.decision_function(xy).reshape(xx.shape)
Z_lr = lr.decision_function(xy).reshape(xx.shape)

ax.contour(xx, yy, Z_svm, colors='black', levels=[0], linestyles=['-'])
ax.contour(xx, yy, Z_lr, colors='orange', levels=[0], linestyles=['-'])

handles = [
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='black', linestyle='-', label='SVM (Hinge Loss)'),
    plt.Line2D([0], [0], color='orange', linestyle='-', label='Logistic Regression (Log Loss)')
]
plt.legend(handles=handles)
plt.title('Linear SVM vs. Logistic Regression')
plt.xlabel('Standardized thalach')
plt.ylabel('Standardized oldpeak')
plt.show()

Both are straight lines and have minor differences. Hinge loss only "cares" about points within the margin, while logistic loss considers all points (scaling inversely to their distance to the margin)

# ii)
gamma_val = 1.0
rbf_svc = SVC(kernel='rbf', gamma=gamma_val, C=1.0)
rbf_svc.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

x_star = np.array([[10.0, 10.0]])

dual_coef = rbf_svc.dual_coef_[0] 
sv = rbf_svc.support_vectors_
b = rbf_svc.intercept_[0]

sq_dists = np.sum((sv - x_star) ** 2, axis=1)
k_vals = np.exp(-gamma_val * sq_dists)

h_x_star = np.sum(dual_coef * k_vals) + b

print(f"h(x*): {h_x_star:.8f}")
print(f"Intercept (b): {b:.8f}")

h(x*): 0.23670193
Intercept (b): 0.23670193

The magnitude of h(x*) is extremely close to b. That means the model has no confidence on how to classify x and "chooses" to make a blind guess of +b.
